name: San Martín Peras Mixtec
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 9 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hedding, Andrew A. 2022. How to Move a Focus: The Syntax of Alternative Particles. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Cruz. §3.5.3 'Against right-headed prominence'. Supporting: Eischens, Ben & Andrew A. Hedding. 2024. San Martín Peras Mixtec (Illustration of the IPA). JIPA 54(2): 811–852, §3.3; Eischens, Ben & Ryan T. Bennett. 2025. The Mixtec couplet is not a consistent grammatical unit. Glossa (lingbuzz/009245 preprint), §3.1–3.2; Eischens, Benjamin J. 2022. Tone, Phonation, and the Phonology-Phonetics Interface in San Martín Peras Mixtec. PhD dissertation, UC Santa Cruz (silent on SMPM word stress).
catalog_locator: Hedding 2022 pp. 176–177 and fn. 13. Tone inventory: Eischens & Hedding 2024 §3.3 'Lexical Tone'. Foot headedness: Eischens & Bennett 2025 preprint.
catalog_quote: In order to show that the SMPM is right-headed with respect to prosody, one would have to demonstrate two things: (1) the final syllable within the word is most prominent; (2) the rightmost word within the phrase is most prominent. ... Some support for the first claim comes from DiCanio et al. (2018), who argue for fixed final stress in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec. ... So, despite the fact that some Mixtec languages have been argued to have final stress, there is no typological basis for claiming that is a common feature of Mixtec languages. More work needs to be done to determine the stress pattern of SMPM.13 Despite the fact that it is plausible that SMPM might have final stress, I argue that there is no evidence that adjectives are more prominent than the nouns they modify in basic cases. That is, there is no evidence that the rightmost word within the phrase is most prominent. ... In fact, neither word appears to be more prominent, which may indicate that ϕ are unheaded in the language. [fn. 13] It is possible that the general restriction of rising tones to word final position is indicative of final stress in the language. However, I don’t think this is the only possible explanation. ... If this hypothesis is correct, then it may offer an alternative explanation for why rising tones are restricted to final position, without appealing to word stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Additionally, in their typology of Mixtec stress patterns DiCanio and Bennett (2020) include seven languages with root-initial str…
new_statements.rule_in_words: San Martín Peras Mixtec (the west2643 dialect all modern phonology treats) is a tone language (H, M, L, LH, HL; mora = TBU) with a right-aligned bimoraic foot (the 'couplet'); no source assigns a word-stress position. Hedding 2022 states outright that the stress pattern of SMPM remains to be determined: final stress is 'plausible' (rising tones are confined to the word-final position) but not established, and phrase-level prominence is not rightmost-headed. Eischens & Bennett 2025 (lingbuzz p. 13) likewise leave open 'whether feet are taken to be trochaic or iambic in SMP Mixtec', i.e. whether the stressed mora is the penultimate or the final one of the foot. The only measured prominence (Hedding 2021) is focus-driven pitch raising of a word-final High tone with no durational correlate.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Hedding's fn. 13 offers a historical (sandhi-fossilization) explanation for final-position rising tones as an alternative to final stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/couplet level: Hedding's discussion concerns the final syllable within the word vs. the rightmost word within the phrase; his phrase-level test (noun + adjective, 64 sentences) found no difference in H-tone pitch between the two words. Eischens & Bennett discuss the foot within the prosodic word (roots plus vocalic enclitics).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted material describes San Martín Peras Mixtec (Glottolog dialect sanm1291 of west2643; Ethnologue places it in jmx; Eischens & Hedding's consultants are from Ahuejutla and the San Martín Peras cabecera). The San Juan Piñas sources (sanj1280 in Glottolog) self-identify with ISO vmc, so their assignment to west2643 rests on Glottolog, not on the authors. The Silacayoapan Mixtec items Glottolog lists under west2643 (Shields 1988; North & Shields 1976/1977) describe a separate language (sila1250, ISO mks). No source of any kind was found for the Coicoyán (coic1238) dialect beyond the unopened Beatham & Beatham 2019 orthography proposal.

tone_statements.citation: Eischens, Benjamin J. 2022. Tone, Phonation, and the Phonology-Phonetics Interface in San Martín Peras Mixtec. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Cruz. 313 pp. eScholarship qt6sq4z7cm.
tone_statements.quote: SJPM has three level tones: H (V5 ), M (V3 ), and L (V1 ), as shown in (2).1 Furthermore, rising contours are attested in lexical tone melodies—e.g. in the first syllable of the root in (3a-c) and in the second syllable in (3d). In contrast, falling contours are attested only in derived environments. … the Tone-Bearing-Unit (TBU) in SJPM is the mora: bimoraic forms (whether monosyllabic or disyllabic) sponsor up to four tones … while monomoraic forms sponsor up to two tones … Altogether, we have identified thus far 16 lexical melodies in monomorphemic bimoraic roots.
tone_statements.locator: p. 295, §2 'Overview of the San Juan Piñas Mixtec tone system'
tone_statements.summary: San Juan Piñas variety: three level tones H, M, L; mora is the TBU and may bear two tones (lexical rising, falling only derived); 16 melodies on bimoraic roots; floating tones mark tense/negation.

tone_statements.citation: Cisneros, Carlos. 2019. Definiteness in Cuevas Mixtec. In Aguilar-Guevara, Pozas Loyo & Vázquez-Rojas Maldonado (eds.), Definiteness across languages, ch. 2. Berlin: Language Science Press.
tone_statements.quote: Otomanguean languages are well known for the preponderance of suprasegmental features, and Cuevas Mixtec is no exception. ... Cuevas Mixtec is also a highly tonal language, with three level tones that combine into nine possible contours. High tones, low tones, and mid tones are marked with acute accent á, grave accent à, and macron ā, respectively. With the help of more recent work on similar varieties of Mixtec (Carroll 2015), I have also been able to identify the presence of floating tones. [fn. 9:] Floating tones are applied to the first vowel of the following word ... They manifest as high tones when the tone of the last vowel is low and as low tones otherwise.
tone_statements.locator: §3.2 'Orthography of Cuevas Mixtec', pp. 53-54 (tone passage top of p.54; footnote 9 on p.54)
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L, marked on every vowel (tone written only on vowel symbols); level tones combine into nine possible two-tone sequences ('contours') on a word; floating tones exist (after Carroll 2015 for related varieties), realized on the first vowel of the following word as H when the source word ends in L and as L otherwise; distribution of floating tones not fully investigated by th…

sources.note: §3.5.3 'Against right-headed prominence', pp. 176–177 + fn. 13: cites DiCanio et al. 2018 (final stress in Yoloxóchitl) and DiCanio & Bennett's Mixtec typology (7 root-initial, 4 final, 3 variable), concludes 'More work needs to be done to determine the stress pattern of SMPM'; final stress 'plausible' (rising tones restricted to word-final position) but offered an alternative historical explanation 'without appealing to word stress'; no evidence that the rightmost word in a phrase is more prominent (ϕ possibly unheaded).

tone.quote: These languages are all tonal and tone carries a high functional load both in lexicon and grammar. Tones in Mixtec are old and must be reconstructed to proto-Mixtec and proto-Mixtecan … The tone-bearing unit (TBU) in Mixtec is the mora, which means that each ‘couplet’ has two tones. These two tones can be level or contour tones, depending on the variety. … Group 7.3 (Josserand’s (1983) Guerrero and Southern Baja area) is split, with the majority of reflexes showing a raising effect, but a minority a lowering effect.
tone.summary: Comparative study of tone change in 42 Mixtec varieties: all Mixtec is tonal, the mora bears tone, two tones per couplet; no inventory for San Martín Peras, which is not in the sample (Coicoyán is).
